Create your first array.simple: Socho tumhare paas paanch chocolate hain aur tum unka total nikalna chahte ho. Python list me har chocolate alag pocket me hai; np.array unhe ek hi dabbe me line se rakh deta hai. Ab total, average ya shape poochhne par NumPy poore dabbe par ek saath kaam karta hai, ek-ek chocolate uthane ki zaroorat nahi.
Create your first array.pro: np.array converts a Python sequence into an ndarray: one contiguous, typed buffer whose shape and values travel together. Because the data is homogeneous and contiguous, reductions and elementwise operations run in compiled loops rather than Python-level iteration, which is why a.mean() and a.shape are O(n) and O(1) respectively instead of a hand-written accumulator.

Vectorised arithmetic.simple: Vectorised ka matlab: ek hi instruction me poori list par kaam. `a * 2` likho to NumPy har number ko double kar deta hai, tumhe `for` loop likhne ki zaroorat nahi. Jaise teacher poori class ko ek saath 'page 10 kholo' bolti hai, har bachche ko alag se nahi.
Vectorised arithmetic.pro: A ufunc applies a scalar or array operand to every element through a compiled loop, so `a * 2` allocates one output array and performs no Python bytecode per element. The win is both asymptotic constant factor and cache-friendly traversal; it does not change the big-O of the operation itself, which is still linear in the number of elements.

Typed memory, not a Python list.simple: Python list me har cheez apni jagah baithi hoti hai — number, text, kuch bhi — isliye list ko har item ka address yaad rakhna padta hai. NumPy array me sab items ek hi type ke hote hain, isliye wo ek compact box jaisa hota hai aur `nbytes` se pata chal jata hai kitni jagah le raha hai.
Typed memory, not a Python list.pro: An ndarray stores homogeneous elements in one buffer with a fixed itemsize; a Python list stores pointers to separately allocated objects plus per-object overhead. That is why nbytes is exact for an array while sys.getsizeof(list) only counts the pointer array, and why dtype changes trade range and precision against memory.

Two arrays combine elementwise.simple: Do arrays ko `+` karne par NumPy unhe jodta nahi, balki ghar-ghar jaakar jodta hai: pehla number pehle se, doosra doosre se. Isliye `[1, 2] + [10, 20]` ka answer `[11, 22]` aata hai, `[1, 2, 10, 20]` nahi — wo list wala kaam hai.
Two arrays combine elementwise.pro: Binary ufuncs pair operands by position when their shapes broadcast, producing an array of the broadcast result shape. Addition is therefore not concatenation; concatenation is a separate reshaping operation (np.concatenate) with its own axis argument.

Indexing starts at zero.simple: Ginti 0 se shuru hoti hai, 1 se nahi. Pehla item `a[0]` hai, doosra `a[1]`, aur last item `a[-1]` se bhi mil jata hai. Ye rule Python list jaisa hi hai, isliye list wali aadat yahan bhi kaam karti hai.
Indexing starts at zero.pro: Indexing is zero-based and negative indices count from the end, exactly as in Python sequences; on an ndarray the same rule generalises per axis for multidimensional arrays. Basic indexing returns a view, not a copy, so writes through the index mutate the original buffer.

Methods return plain results.simple: `a.sum()` ya `a.max()` likhne par jawab ek simple number hota hai, poora array nahi. Us number ko tum seedha print kar sakte ho, compare kar sakte ho, ya kisi doosre kaam me daal sakte ho.
Methods return plain results.pro: Reduction methods return NumPy scalars (or arrays when axis is given), not Python ints/floats; they behave like numbers in arithmetic and printing but carry a dtype. Use axis to reduce along one dimension and keepdims to preserve rank for broadcasting against the original array.

Convert back to a Python list.simple: Kabhi kisi function ko NumPy array nahi, simple list chahiye hoti hai. Tab `a.tolist()` use karo — array wahi rehta hai, bas uski list wali copy mil jati hai jise koi bhi Python code samajh leta hai.
Convert back to a Python list.pro: tolist() recursively converts an ndarray to nested Python lists, turning NumPy scalars into native ints/floats. It is a copy, so later changes to the array do not appear in the list; it is the right boundary when an API requires plain Python containers or JSON serialisation.

Integers and floats carry different dtyp.simple: Agar tum `np.array([1, 2])` likhte ho to NumPy sochta hai 'ye pure number hain' aur integer array banata hai — isme 2.5 nahi rakha ja sakta. `[1.0, 2.0]` likho to float array banta hai, jo decimal sambhal leta hai.
Integers and floats carry different dtyp.pro: dtype is inferred from the input values: an all-integer sequence yields a platform int (int64 on 64-bit), a sequence containing a float yields float64. Integer arrays cannot hold fractional values without an explicit cast, and casting a float to an integer truncates toward zero.

Add a scalar to every element.simple: Ek number ko poore array me jodna ho to bas `a + 5` likho. NumPy us 5 ko har cell me pahucha deta hai — yehi broadcasting ka sabse chhota example hai.
Add a scalar to every element.pro: Broadcasting stretches the scalar across every position without materialising a repeated array, so `a + 5` is a single ufunc call over the buffer. Because no temporary of the array's shape is created for the scalar, the extra memory cost is the output array only.

Compare an array with a scalar.simple: `a > 10` likhne par tumhe True/False ka array milta hai — har number ke liye ek jawab. Yahi boolean mask aage filtering ka poora base banta hai: mask ke andar jahan True hai, wahi values chunti hain.
Compare an array with a scalar.pro: Comparison ufuncs return a bool array of the broadcast shape rather than a single truth value, which is why `if a > 10:` must be replaced by `.any()` or `.all()`. The mask is then used for boolean indexing, where True positions select elements and the result is a copy.

A Python loop still works over an array.simple: Array par normal `for` loop bhi chal jata hai — wo ek-ek karke values deta hai. Chhote data par theek hai, lekin lakhon numbers par ye dheema pad jata hai, kyunki tab kaam Python karta hai, NumPy nahi.
A Python loop still works over an array.pro: Iteration over an ndarray yields subarrays along the first axis and executes Python-level bytecode per step, which dominates cost at scale. Prefer vectorised expressions or reductions; where a loop is unavoidable, keep the body minimal and consider np.frompyfunc or compiled helpers rather than per-element Python calls.

Every array reports its own type.simple: `np.array(...)` hamesha ek `ndarray` deta hai. Python list aur ndarray ek jaise dikhte hain, par same cheez nahi hain — list me `.mean()` nahi hota, aur ndarray me list wale kuch methods nahi hote.
Every array reports its own type.pro: np.array returns an instance of numpy.ndarray (a subclass such as np.matrix is deprecated for new code), and type checks should use isinstance(value, np.ndarray). Lists and arrays are not interchangeable: arrays expose dtype, shape and strides, while lists expose list methods; conversion is explicit via np.asarray or .tolist().
